title: Work with us
text: The lab is part of a federal research centre, which affects the kinds of opportunities we can offer. We do not handle graduate admissions. You can still work with us through the Research Affiliate Program.

title: Work with us
text:
Students
We take undergraduate co-op students, summer students and honours project students, and co-supervise graduate students with university supervisors. Recent projects include pedigree visualization, genomic selection pipelines and real-time nanopore analysis.
The problems are a blend of mathematics, software engineering and genomics. You should have a background in either life sciences, computer science or mathematics, and be willing to work across the other two.
What matters is not how much code you can write by hand. It is critical thinking, an engineering mindset, and accountability for a result. If you can define the problem cleanly and stay with it until something actually works for a breeder, that is the job.

title: Work with us
text:
Breeders and research scientists
If you have a data problem, such as a pipeline that only runs on one person’s laptop, a genotype file you cannot join to your field book, or an analysis you would rather run yourself, that is the core of the job, not a favour. Get in touch early, rather than after the data is collected. The design decisions that make analysis easier are usually made before anything is sequenced.

title: Work with us
text:
Collaborations
We work with groups across AAFC, universities and industry on population genomics and breeding data. If your problem sits somewhere between genomics, mathematics and software engineering, that is generally where we are most useful.

Getting in touch
Email tayab.soomro@agr.gc.ca. For student enquiries, say what you want to work on and roughly when you are available. Include a CV with student enquiries.
For project enquiries, one paragraph about the question and one about the available data are enough to get started.


What happens next. We read every enquiry. If there is a fit, we will suggest a short conversation about the question, the data and timing.

title: Tayab Soomro
text:
Data Scientist Lead (Bioinformatics)
I lead data science at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada’s Brandon Research and Development Centre. Breeders already collect the data; the bottleneck is turning it into a decision. I work with breeders on those decisions, and I build the tools that remove what is in the way.
My route in was through computer science rather than biology, and that has shaped what I work on. The problems I find interesting are engineering problems standing between a breeder and an answer they could already have.

title: Soomro Lab
text:
Soomro Lab · Brandon Research and Development Centre · Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

Breeding programs are rarely limited by biology. They are limited by the distance between the data they collect and the decisions they make.

We shorten that distance. We are the bioinformatics group at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada’s Brandon Research and Development Centre. We support breeders and research scientists with genomics and computational biology, and we build connected breeding data and analysis pipelines that do not need a bioinformatician standing beside them.
Two current examples: a genomic selection pipeline now run by the barley breeding program itself, and nanoCAS, a real-time nanopore diagnostic built for the field.
Weather is getting less predictable faster than variety development cycles can absorb, and the crops going into the ground now have to survive conditions nobody bred them for. Breeding is how agriculture adapts. Our job is to remove whatever is slowing it down.
These bottlenecks (e.g., disconnected data, unclear marker–trait relationships, analysis queued behind one person) recur across wheat, barley, oat, canola and pulses, so we build tools that work across crop types.
The lab is led by Tayab Soomro, and most of what we build is released openly.

title: Software
text:
These are tools we have released publicly. They are free to install and run.
We also maintain pipelines for breeding programs at Brandon that are not public. They stay inside the centre because they are connected to program data.

Open tools

nanoCAS Manuscript in preparation
Real-time detection and decision making during nanopore sequencing
Nanopore sequencing produces reads as it goes, but most analysis still waits for the run to finish. nanoCAS treats the run as a stream: it watches reads arrive, classifies them against a target database, and raises a detection as soon as there is enough evidence. For a field diagnostic, that can mean an answer in minutes rather than at the end of a flow cell.
It ships with a web interface so the person running the sample does not need a terminal.

Nextflow pipeline for genomic selection in barley

title: Research
text: Four threads, one problem. A breeding program generates enormous amounts of information — pedigree, genotype, phenotype, environment, disease pressure — and then struggles to ask questions that cross more than one of those categories at a time. Everything below is an attempt to make one of those crossings cheap.

title: Research
text:
Connected breeding data
In most breeding programs information lives in disconnected systems: pedigrees in one database, genotypes in another, field notes in spreadsheets, environmental data somewhere else again. Any question spanning two of them becomes a manual joining exercise, which means most such questions never get asked.
We model breeding data as a graph instead — lines, parents, markers, haplotypes, environments and traits as entities, with the relationships between them stored explicitly and queried directly. That turns which high-yielding lines carry this haplotype while still retaining diversity from the rest of the program? into a query rather than a week of work.
The first application is pedigree visualization for wheat: panning through a crop pedigree coloured by trait, so you can see how a trait moves through a set of crosses, overlay KASP marker calls, and check whether a marker is genuinely driving the phenotype or merely travelling near it. Further out, the same integrated data is the groundwork for a digital twin of a breeding program — a model connecting genomics, pedigree, environment and field performance well enough to evaluate candidate crosses before growing them out.

title: Research
section: Diagnostics that run where the crop is
text:
Diagnostics that run where the crop is
Conventional pathogen testing means shipping a sample to a lab and waiting days for an answer. By the time it arrives the decision has usually been made without it, often as a broad fungicide application.
We work on closing that loop with portable nanopore sequencing. nanoCAS is an event-driven framework that watches a sequencing run as it happens and makes detection calls in real time, rather than waiting for the run to finish and the analysis to be queued. Paired with the Mk1C, that puts a sequencing-grade diagnostic in a truck.
Targets so far span plant and animal systems: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum in canola, Xylella fastidiosa in grapevine, Brucella abortus in cattle and Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae in sheep.

title: Research
text:
Trait discovery and population genomics
The support side of the lab and the innovation side meet here. We run genome-wide association studies in Vicia faba populations for rust resistance and heat tolerance, and QTL analysis in bi-parental wheat populations — using the pedigree to trace which markers came down from which parent, then asking which progeny carry both the markers and the trait.
We also contribute to comparative genomics of Aphanomyces euteiches, the root rot pathogen of pulse crops, where better annotation is the prerequisite for understanding pathogenicity and host resistance.

title: Research
section: Pipelines people can run without us
text:
Pipelines people can run without us
A bioinformatics group becomes a bottleneck the moment every analysis has to pass through it. So a standing goal is to build pipelines that are self-contained, independently runnable and documented well enough that someone can pick one up without handholding.
The working proof is a genomic selection pipeline that any member of the barley breeding program can now run themselves. The same approach is being extended across the Brandon and Morden bioinformatics groups so that discrete, well-specified tasks can move to whoever has capacity — and so that routine analysis stops competing with new work for the same hours.

Software

nanoCAS — event-driven framework for real-time detection during nanopore sequencing
MICAS — MinION classification and alerting system
genoassist — genome assembly and annotation framework that compares assemblies so you can pick the best one
BiocSwirl — interactive R/Bioconductor courses for teaching bioinformatics workflows
